question: Y127
answer:
LEGAL NOTE — s.378 Companies Act 2006 (c. 46), Part 14 'Exemptions': the small-donations exception

1. QUESTION
In the text of s.378 stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026, what donation ceiling and what measuring period does the section state?

2. SHORT ANSWER
(a) Ceiling: £5,000.
(b) Measuring period: the period of 12 months ending with the date on which the donation is made — i.e. a rolling 12-month look-back tested at the date of each donation, not the company's financial year, not a calendar year, and not a fixed authorisation period.
The ceiling is an aggregate (group-wide) threshold, not a per-donation limit: the donation plus 'other relevant donations' in that 12-month window must together exceed £5,000 before authorisation under Part 14 is required, and then only to the extent of the excess.

3. VERSION AND CURRENCY (discharging the 'up to date through 20 November 2026' constraint)
Source used: legislation.gov.uk, Companies Act 2006, s.378, 'Latest available (Revised)' rendition — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378 (page fetched 23 Nov 2026; sha256 e6f01f42e1ef), corroborated by the Part 14 data view (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/data.html, sha256 a394eec543f0).
The page's own currency statement reads: 'Companies Act 2006, Section 378 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026. There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date.'
23 November 2026 is later than the requested 20 November 2026 cut-off, so this rendition includes and therefore states the position on 20 November 2026. There is no separate '20 November 2026' snapshot on the site; the point-in-time alternatives offered for s.378 are 1 October 2007 and 12 October 2022.
Cross-check against the 12 October 2022 point-in-time version (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2022-10-12, sha256 c4c6cb90b6c5): the operative text of s.378 — subsections (1) to (3) — is word-for-word identical to the latest rendition, including '£5,000' and 'the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made'. So no amendment between 12 October 2022 and 23 November 2026 altered either figure.
Outstanding (not yet in force) changes: the entry visible on the s.378 page is 'Sch. 11A para. 17E-17G substituted for Sch. 11A para. 17A-17D by 2026 c. 23 Sch. 36 para. 35' — a Schedule 11A matter, not s.378, and in any event not in force on the relevant date.
Commencement/modification annotations on the section: s.378 wholly in force at 1 October 2008 (in force for certain purposes 1 October 2007 E.W.S. and 1 November 2007 N.I.) by S.I. 2007/2194; and ss.362–379 applied with modifications to unregistered companies from 1 October 2009 by The Unregistered Companies Regulations 2009 (S.I. 2009/2436), Sch. 1 para. 9. Neither annotation alters the £5,000 or the 12-month measure.

4. VERBATIM TEXT RELIED ON (s.378 as reproduced in the rendition above)
'378 Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period
U.K.
(1) Authorisation under this Part is not needed for a donation except to the extent that the total amount of—
(a) that donation, and
(b) other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made,
exceeds £5,000.
(2) In this section—
"donation" means a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate; and
"other relevant donations" means—
(a) in relation to a donation made by a company that is not a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company or by any of its subsidiaries;
(b) in relation to a donation made by a company that is a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company, by any holding company of that company or by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.
(3) If or to the extent that a donation is exempt by virtue of this section from the requirement of authorisation under this Part, it shall be disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by any resolution passed for the purposes of this Part.'

5. POINTS OF CONSTRUCTION A COMPANY SECRETARY SHOULD NOT MISS
5.1 Aggregate, not per-donation. The test is not 'is this donation £5,000 or less?'. It is whether the running total of this donation plus other relevant donations in the trailing 12 months exceeds £5,000. A £4,000 donation is exempt only if no more than £1,000 of other relevant donations was made in the preceding 12 months.
5.2 Only the excess needs authorisation. The words 'except to the extent that ... exceeds £5,000' mean the first £5,000 of aggregate donations in the rolling window falls outside the authorisation requirement; the balance does not.
5.3 Group aggregation. For a company that is not a subsidiary, donations by it and by any of its subsidiaries count. For a subsidiary, donations by it, by any holding company of it, and by any other subsidiary of any such holding company count. The threshold is therefore effectively a single group-wide rolling allowance, not one per company.
5.4 Rolling, not financial-year. The measure is 'the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made'. The company's accounting reference date is irrelevant to the s.378 test. Do not use the financial year, and do not use the calendar year used for PPERA 2000 reporting. Each donation is tested against its own trailing 12 months, so the allowance is continuously rolling rather than resetting annually.
5.5 What the date of a donation is. The section keys the window to 'the date on which that donation is made'. Section 379(2) is annotated as containing the construction of references to the date when a donation is made or expenditure incurred, so the operative date is to be determined under s.379 rather than by ordinary accounting convention. I have not been given the verbatim text of s.379 in this exercise and do not quote it; it should be read before applying the window to a donation whose timing is arguable (e.g. a pledge, a loan, or a donation made through an intermediary).
5.6 Meaning of 'donation'. Section 378(2) defines 'donation' for its own purposes as a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate. This is not the same defined term as 'political donation' used elsewhere in Part 14 (s.364, which incorporates ss.50–52 PPERA 2000 with the Electoral Administration Act 2006 amendments to loans disregarded). The Explanatory Notes confirm the lineage: 'section 378 restates the exemption in section 347B of the 1985 Act under which authorisation for donations is not required unless the donation or aggregate amount of the donations by the company exceeds £5,000 in a 12 month period. Donations by other group companies (including subsidiaries) must be taken into account in calculating whether the £5,000 threshold has been exceeded.'
5.7 Effect of exemption. Under s.378(3), a donation exempt under the section is disregarded when determining what donations are authorised by a members' resolution under Part 14 — so exempt donations neither consume nor count against a resolution's authority.
5.8 What the exception is not. Section 378 exempts only from the requirement of authorisation under Part 14. It does not exempt from anything else — in particular not from reporting obligations under PPERA 2000 / the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act regime, nor from the separate authorisation requirements of Part 14 where the aggregate does exceed £5,000. The ceiling is stated in the Act as a fixed sum; s.378 itself contains no indexation mechanism and no power to vary the figure by order, so the £5,000 stands unless the Act is amended.
5.9 Contrast with the authorisation period. Do not confuse the s.378 measuring period with the maximum life of an approval resolution under s.368 (not more than four years). They are different periods serving different functions.

6. HOW TO RE-VERIFY (should a later reader need to)
(i) Open https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378 and read the 'Changes to legislation' statement — confirm the stated currency date is on or after the cut-off date required. (ii) Check the 'Alternative versions' / point-in-time list for any version between the last known change and the cut-off, and compare subsections (1)–(3) word for word. (iii) Check the 'Changes and effects yet to be applied' list attached to s.378 for anything touching s.378 itself, as opposed to other provisions. (iv) Read s.379 for the construction of 'the date when a donation is made' before applying the window to any donation with arguable timing.

7. STATUS OF THIS NOTE
This is a statement of what the enacted text says, prepared in the Legal Counsel function. It is legal information about a statutory provision, not legal advice on any particular company's donations, and it is not a substitute for advice on the facts of a live case (in particular on whether a particular payment is a 'donation' within s.378(2) and on when it is treated as made under s.379).

8. CITED SOURCES
- Companies Act 2006, s.378, latest available (revised) rendition, legislation.gov.uk, fetched 23 Nov 2026, sha256 e6f01f42e1ef.
- Companies Act 2006, s.378, point in time 12 Oct 2022, sha256 c4c6cb90b6c5.
- Companies Act 2006, Part 14 data view (s.378 text with annotations), sha256 a394eec543f0.
- Companies Act 2006, Table of Contents (s.378 heading), sha256 3459f0e70ddd.
- Explanatory Notes to the Companies Act 2006, Part 14 commentary (note on s.378), sha256 a8b7a2feacc4.

question: Y128
answer:
# Section 586, Companies Act 2006 (c. 46) — minimum paid-up fraction on allotment by a public company

## 1. Answer

**One-quarter (1/4 = 25%) of the nominal value of the share, plus the whole (100%) of any premium on it.**

Section 586(1) does *not* set a flat 25% of the issue price. It sets two components:

- **25% of nominal value** (par value), and
- **100% of any premium** (share premium).

So on a £1.00 nominal share issued at £1.50 (50p premium), the minimum paid up at allotment is £0.25 + £0.50 = **£0.75**, not £0.375. The 25% applies to nominal value only; the premium is not discounted.

## 2. Statutory text relied on

Section 586 ("Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up"), as in force and unamended through 20 November 2026:

> **586 Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up**
>
> (1) A public company must not allot a share except as paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value and the whole of any premium on it.
>
> (2) This does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.
>
> (3) If a company allots a share in contravention of this section—
> (a) the share is to be treated as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on it, had been received, and
> (b) the allottee is liable to pay the company the minimum amount which should have been received in respect of the share under subsection (1) (less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, to any extent, of the share and any premium on it), with interest at the appropriate rate.
>
> (4) Subsection (3) does not apply to the allotment of bonus shares, unless the allottee knew or ought to have known the shares were allotted in contravention of this section.

## 3. Currency of the text — satisfaction of the 20 November 2026 constraint

Source: legislation.gov.uk, revised version of the Act (UK Public General Acts, 2006 c. 46, Part 17, Chapter 5), section 586.

- The latest-available revised view states: *"Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026. There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date."* A statement current to 23 November 2026 necessarily incorporates every change in force on or before **20 November 2026**; the constraint is therefore met (a point-in-time view on the same site carries 22 November 2026, which is likewise a superset of the required date).
- The operative words of s.586(1) are **identical** in the King's Printer as-enacted text, the 1 October 2009 version, the 26 June 2017 point-in-time version and the latest-available revised version. Section 586 was brought into force on 1 October 2009 and **subsection (1) has never been amended**.
- Outstanding editorial material on the s.586 page — *"Sch. 11A para. 17E-17G substituted for Sch. 11A para. 17A-17D by 2026 c. 23 Sch. 36 para. 35"* — affects Schedule 11A, not section 586. No prospective change to the one-quarter figure is recorded.
- Only non-textual modifications exist: application of ss.584–587 by S.I. 2009/1941, Sch. 3, para. 9 (from 1.10.2009) and S.I. 2011/1265, Sch. 1, para. 9 (from 12.5.2011); and the bank-resolution modification in S.I. 2014/3348, Sch. 4, Part 3, para. 32, which substitutes s.586(2) for companies under resolution under Part 17 of the Bank Recovery and Resolution (No. 2) Order 2014. None touches subsection (1).

The figure is therefore stable across every version of the provision from enactment to the cut-off date, so the answer is unaffected by the two-to-three-day difference between the requested date and the site's editorial statement.

## 4. Arithmetic — computing the minimum

Let **N** = nominal value per share and **P** = premium per share. Minimum amount to be paid up at allotment, per share:

**Minimum = 0.25 × N + P**

| N (nominal) | P (premium) | Minimum paid up | As % of N | As % of total price (N+P) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| £1.00 | £0.00 | £0.25 | 25% | 25% |
| £1.00 | £0.50 | £0.75 | 75% | 50% |
| £0.10 | £0.00 | £0.025 | 25% | 25% |
| £1.00 | £4.00 | £4.25 | 425% | 85% |

As a proportion of the total subscription price the requirement is 0.25 + 0.75P/(N+P), which is 25% when there is no premium and rises towards (but never reaches) 100% as the premium increases. It is never correct to describe the rule as "25% of the issue price".

## 5. Compliance points a public company must observe

1. **Identify N and P** from the allotment resolution / articles. Where shares are of no par value in a foreign sense — not applicable to CA 2006 companies — nominal value is always stated; every CA 2006 share has one.
2. **Pay up at allotment, not merely call up.** The section prohibits allotment "except as paid up" to the minimum. A promise to pay, an unpaid call, or a subscriber's liability under the articles is not enough. The consideration must actually be applied in paying up the share and premium (s.586(3)(b) expressly deducts "the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up").
3. **Non-cash consideration.** For a public company, s.593 requires an independent valuation of non-cash consideration before allotment; the valued consideration must then be applied in paying up the share and premium. s.586 and s.593 operate together — s.586 sets the amount, s.593 the manner of proof.
4. **Employees' share scheme exemption.** s.586(2) disapplies the minimum for shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme (defined for the Companies Acts in s.1166). The exemption is scheme-specific; it does not cover ad hoc employee allotments outside a scheme.
5. **Bonus shares.** s.586(4) disapplies the s.586(3) consequences for bonus shares unless the allottee knew or ought to have known of the contravention — it does not disapply subsection (1) itself.
6. **Consequence of shortfall.** The allotment is **not void**. Under s.586(3)(a) the share is treated as if one-quarter of nominal value plus the whole premium had been received, and under s.586(3)(b) the allottee is personally liable to the company for the shortfall, with interest at the appropriate rate, credit being given for consideration actually applied.
7. **Bank resolution carve-out.** For a company under resolution for the purposes of Part 17 of the Bank Recovery and Resolution (No. 2) Order 2014, S.I. 2014/3348, Sch. 4, para. 32 substitutes s.586(2) so that the section does not apply to shares allotted by use of resolution tools, powers and mechanisms. (The substituted text as published refers to an "employers' share scheme", apparently a typographical rendering of "employees'".) This carve-out does not alter the s.586(1) figure for ordinary allotments.
8. **Scope.** Section 586 applies by its terms to public companies only. A private company is outside it, but on re-registration as a public company every subsequent allotment falls within it.

## 6. Audit trail

- Provision: Companies Act 2006, s.586(1).
- Fraction: **one-quarter of nominal value (0.25 / 25%) plus the whole of any premium (100%)**.
- Version: legislation.gov.uk revised text, stated up to date with all changes in force on or before 23 November 2026 — covers the requested 20 November 2026 cut-off; s.586(1) unamended since commencement on 1 October 2009.
- Corroboration: the same wording appears in the King's Printer as-enacted text and in the LexisNexis reproduction of the section.
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 23 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2017-06-26 and 22 on legislation.gov.uk/cy/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2009-10-01. The first reads: "Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026."
The answer gives 0.25 for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y129
answer:
WORD LIMITS FOR MOTION MEMORANDA — FTC ADJUDICATIVE PROCEEDINGS, 16 CFR PART 3 AS IN FORCE 2026-11-21

AUTHORITY AND DATE CHECK
Governing provision: 16 CFR § 3.22(c) (Subpart C — Pleadings, Motions, and Other Matters; motion practice before the Administrative Law Judge and the Commission).
Text verified against (a) the 2026 annual edition of the CFR, 16 CFR part 3 (govinfo, CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.pdf, page-stamp 'VerDate Sep<11>2014 11:35 Aug 25, 2026', i.e. the printed 2026 edition) and (b) the eCFR 'current' point-in-time pages for part 3, retrieved 2026-11-23T10:46Z — two days after the requested operative date of 2026-11-21. The two sources are identical as to the figures below; no amendment between the 2026 annual edition and the post-2026-11-21 eCFR snapshot changes § 3.22(c). Section source note appearing with § 3.22: '[74 FR 1821, Jan. 13, 2009, as amended at 80 FR 15160, Mar. 23, 2015].'

THE ANSWER
| Filing | Word limit |
|---|---|
| Memorandum in support of a dispositive motion | 10,000 words |
| Memorandum in opposition to a dispositive motion | 10,000 words |
| Memorandum in support of any other (non-dispositive) motion | 2,500 words |
| Memorandum in opposition to any other (non-dispositive) motion | 2,500 words |

Supporting and opposing memoranda share a single limit in each category; § 3.22(c) says 'in support of, or in opposition to' in one clause, so there is no separate, lower or higher figure for an opposition memorandum.

VERBATIM TEXT OF § 3.22(c)
'(c) Content. All written motions shall state the particular order, ruling, or action desired and the grounds therefor. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion shall not exceed 2,500 words. Any reply in support of a dispositive motion shall not exceed 5,000 words and any reply in support of any other motion authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission shall not exceed 1,250 words. These word count limitations include headings, footnotes, and quotations, but do not include the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, any addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations, any certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e).'

WHAT COUNTS TOWARD THE LIMIT (express in § 3.22(c))
Counted: headings; footnotes; quotations.
Not counted: the cover; table of contents; table of citations or authorities; glossaries; statements with respect to oral argument; addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations; certificates of counsel; proposed form of order; any attachment required by § 3.45(e) (the confidential/in camera filing attachment).
Note the counting rule is materially broader than the common federal-court practice of exempting footnotes — under § 3.22(c) footnotes and quotations are counted, so the practical ceiling is tighter than 10,000/2,500 words of body text.

ADJACENT LIMITS A PRACTITIONER WILL HIT (reported for completeness; not part of the answer to the two categories asked)
- Replies: 5,000 words (reply in support of a dispositive motion); 1,250 words (reply in support of any other motion, and only where authorized by the ALJ or the Commission). § 3.22(c). Replies to non-dispositive motions are permitted only to draw attention to recent important developments or controlling authority that could not have been raised earlier, and may be conditionally filed with a motion for leave; any reply is due within 5 days after service of the last answer. § 3.22(d).
- Motions under § 3.31 (motion to withdraw the adjudicative proceeding from adjudication; motion to dismiss on public-interest grounds after denial of preliminary injunctive relief): § 3.31(e) independently caps supporting and opposing memoranda at 10,000 words, with the same inclusion/exclusion list. This is consistent with, not a departure from, the § 3.22(c) dispositive-motion figure.
- Applications for review / answers thereto: 2,500 words each, § 3.23(c) — an appellate filing, not a motion; do not import it into motion practice.
- Appeal briefs to the Commission: opening 14,000, answering 14,000, reply 7,000 words, § 3.52(c)-(e), each 'without leave of the Commission'.

EXCEEDING THE LIMIT
Section 3.22(c) is drafted as an absolute cap ('shall not exceed') and, unlike the Commission brief rules in § 3.52 ('shall not, without leave of the Commission, exceed 14,000 words'), contains no express leave-to-exceed or good-cause enlargement clause for motion memoranda. The rule text therefore provides no stated mechanism for an over-length motion memorandum; the safe reading of the text as in force on 2026-11-21 is that 10,000 / 2,500 words are hard ceilings, and any relief would have to come from the presiding ALJ or the Commission outside the four corners of § 3.22(c). Counsel should not plan on an enlargement.

CLASSIFICATION NOTE
Which limit applies turns on whether the motion is 'dispositive.' Section 3.22(c) does not define the term; the Part 3 architecture treats as dispositive, at minimum, motions that terminate the proceeding or a party's claims (e.g., § 3.31 motions to withdraw from adjudication and to dismiss on public-interest grounds, and summary disposition under § 3.24), while discovery, procedural, scheduling, in limine, and similar interlocutory motions fall in the 2,500-word 'any other motion' bucket. Where characterization is contestable, the conservative course is to draft to 2,500 words or to seek the ALJ's guidance before filing.

RELATED PROCEDURAL CONTEXT (same rule, useful for calendaring)
All written motions are filed with the Secretary of the Commission, with a copy to the ALJ at filing; motions addressed to the Commission must be in writing (§ 3.22(a)). A pending Commission motion does not stay proceedings before the ALJ absent a Commission order or contrary rule (§ 3.22(b)). The ALJ rules on motions within 14 days after the last authorized motion paper is filed, subject to extension by the Commission for good cause (§ 3.22(e)). Motions for extensions of time may be excused from § 3.22's requirements, but the ALJ has no authority to rule on ex parte extension motions (§ 3.22(f)). Discovery-related motions (to quash under § 3.34(c); to compel/determine sufficiency, for sanctions, or for enforcement under § 3.38(a)-(c)) require a signed meet-and-confer statement (§ 3.22(g)).

question: Y130
answer:
# Withdrawal period expiry under Directive 2011/83/EU (CELEX 32011L0083)

## 1. The answer in one line

Both periods are **14 days**. The difference is the **trigger day** from which the 14 days run:

| Contract type | Period | Runs from | Provision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sales contract** (trader transfers / undertakes to transfer ownership of goods, incl. contracts mixing goods and services — Art. 2(5)) | 14 days | The day the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, **acquires physical possession of the goods** | Art. 9(1) + Art. 9(2)(a) |
| **Service contract** (any contract other than a sales contract for the supply of a service — Art. 2(6)) | 14 days | The day the **contract is concluded** | Art. 9(1) + Art. 9(2)(c) |

Scope gate to state in the instructions themselves: this right exists only for **distance contracts and off-premises contracts** (Art. 9(1), read with Art. 3(1)). A sale concluded on the trader's premises carries no EU-law withdrawal right, so the clause must not be used indiscriminately across all channels.

## 2. Sub-rules for sales contracts that an online retailer will actually hit

Article 9(2)(a) is not a single trigger; it has three carve-outs. Draft for whichever applies to the product line:

1. **Multiple goods ordered in one order and delivered separately** — the period runs from possession of the **last good**.
2. **A good consisting of multiple lots or pieces** (e.g. a flat-pack or a multi-box set) — the period runs from possession of the **last lot or piece**.
3. **Contracts for the regular delivery of goods during a defined period of time** (subscriptions, box schemes) — the period runs from possession of the **first good**.

Adjacent supplies are treated like services, not goods: contracts for water, gas, electricity or district heating (where not supplied in a limited volume or set quantity) and for **digital content not supplied on a tangible medium** start on the day the contract is concluded (Art. 9(2)(b)); utilities supplied in a limited volume or set quantity also start on conclusion (Art. 9(2)(c)). So a pure download or streaming subscription expires 14 days after checkout, not after any delivery event.

## 3. How the 14 days are counted

Article 9(1) gives a period of "14 days"; the directive does not itself set out a counting method, so the trigger day is **not** counted and the period expires at the **end of the 14th day** (midnight, per the counting rule of the applicable national law). Worked examples, both consistent with the table above:

- **Sales**: goods delivered **Monday 1 September 2025**. Day of delivery not counted. Period runs Tue 2 Sep – Mon 15 Sep 2025; **expires at the end of Monday 15 September 2025**.
- **Service**: contract concluded **Friday 5 September 2025**. Period runs Sat 6 Sep – Fri 19 Sep 2025; **expires at the end of Friday 19 September 2025**.

Dispatch, not receipt, stops the clock for the consumer: the right is exercised in time if the consumer **sends** the communication before the period expires (Art. 11(2)). Say so in the instructions — it is the sentence most often omitted and it is the one that prevents disputes about postal delays.

## 4. When the period is longer than 14 days (Art. 10) — must be reflected in the drafting

The 14 days is the **default**. It is displaced where the trader has not given the withdrawal information required by **Art. 6(1)(h)** (conditions, time limit, procedures, model form):

- **Art. 10(1)**: the period expires **12 months after the end of the initial withdrawal period**.
- **Art. 10(2)**: if the trader supplies that information **within 12 months of the Art. 9(2) trigger day**, the period expires **14 days after the day the consumer receives the information**.

Worked example (sales): goods delivered 1 Sep 2025, no withdrawal information given -> initial period ends 15 Sep 2025 -> extended period ends **15 Sep 2026**. If the information is supplied on 10 Mar 2026, the period instead ends **24 Mar 2026** (14 days later), which sits inside the 15 Sep 2026 outer limit. Information supplied after the outer limit has run does not revive a lapsed right.

The same mechanism applies to service contracts. Practical consequence for the retailer: the Article 10 trap is triggered by the **information** failure, not by the delivery or performance failure, so the withdrawal clause must be checked as part of the pre-contractual information pack, not only as part of the T&Cs.

## 5. When the right is lost or excluded (drafting must say so, or the clause is misleading)

Relevant to the two contract types in the question:

- **Services fully performed (Art. 16(a))**: no right of withdrawal once the service has been fully performed, **if** performance began with the consumer's **prior express consent** and with the consumer's **acknowledgement that the right is lost** on full performance. Both elements must be evidenced; a pre-ticked box will not do.
- **Service begun but not completed, then withdrawn**: the consumer pays an amount **proportionate to what has been supplied** up to the point of withdrawal, and only if performance was requested during the withdrawal period and the required information was given (Art. 14(4)(a), with the Art. 6(1)(j) information on that cost liability).
- **Digital content not on a tangible medium (Art. 16(m))**: right lost once performance has begun with prior express consent and acknowledgement of loss, plus the trader's confirmation under Art. 7(2)/(3).
- Other Art. 16 exclusions commonly triggered online: goods made to the consumer's specifications or clearly personalised; goods liable to deteriorate or expire rapidly; sealed goods unsealed after delivery and not suitable for return for health protection or hygiene reasons; sealed audio/video/software unsealed after delivery; newspapers/periodicals (excluding subscriptions).
- Where no right exists, **Art. 6(1)(k)** requires the trader to say so, and to state the circumstances in which the right is lost.

Also to be reflected: reimbursement is due without undue delay and in any event **within 14 days** of being informed (Art. 13(1)), and for sales contracts the trader may **withhold** reimbursement until the goods are received back or the consumer supplies evidence of return, whichever is earlier (Art. 13(3)). Note the symmetry — 14 days out, 14 days back — because retailers routinely mis-state one of the two.

## 6. Ready-to-use instruction text

Drafting basis: **Art. 8(4)** permits the Art. 6(1)(h)–(j) information to be given using the **model instructions on withdrawal in Annex I(A)**. The text below follows that model. Insert the trader's name, geographical address, telephone number, fax number and e-mail address in the bracketed field. **Check the wording verbatim against Annex I(A) and Annex I(B) before publication** (see §7).

### 6a. Goods — single delivery (sales contract)

> **Right of withdrawal**
> You have the right to withdraw from this contract within 14 days without giving any reason.
> The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the goods.
> To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us [trader name, geographical address, telephone number, fax number and e-mail address] of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (e.g. a letter sent by post, fax or e-mail). You may use the attached model withdrawal form, but it is not obligatory.
> To meet the withdrawal deadline, it is sufficient for you to send your communication concerning your exercise of the right of withdrawal before the withdrawal period has expired.

### 6b. Goods — add where applicable

> In the case of multiple goods ordered by you in one order and delivered separately, the withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of the last good.

### 6c. Services (service contract)

We will not charge you that amount unless we informed you of this liability before you made your request.

### 6d. Effects of withdrawal (common to both)

> **Effects of withdrawal**

We will carry out such reimbursement using the same means of payment as you used for the initial transaction, unless you have expressly agreed otherwise; in any event, you will not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.

You must send back the goods without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which you communicate your withdrawal from this contract to us. The deadline is met if you send back the goods before the period of 14 days has expired. You will bear the direct cost of returning the goods [insert where applicable; if the goods by their nature cannot normally be returned by post, state the cost]. You are only liable for any diminished value of the goods resulting from handling other than what is necessary to establish the nature, characteristics and functioning of the goods.

### 6e. Model withdrawal form (Annex I(B)) — attach to the instructions

> To [trader's name, geographical address, fax number and e-mail address]:
> I/We hereby give notice that I/We withdraw from my/our contract of sale of the following goods / provision of the following service (*)
> Ordered on (*) / received on (*)
> Name of consumer(s)
> Address of consumer(s)
> Signature of consumer(s) (only if this form is notified on paper)
> Date
> (*) Delete as appropriate.

## 7. Provenance and verification before publication

The EUR-Lex text at CELEX 32011L0083 could **not** be retrieved in this working environment, so nothing in this note is presented as a verified verbatim quotation. The substantive rules in §1–§5 are the directive's settled content and can be relied on; the following should be confirmed word-for-word against the official text before the instructions go live:

1. **Annex I(A) model instructions and Annex I(B) model form** — reproduce verbatim; do not paraphrase, because Art. 8(4) compliance depends on using the model.
2. **Article 9(2)(b) vs 9(2)(c) allocation** — confirm which sub-paragraph carries the "not supplied in a limited volume or set quantity" qualifier for utilities. The expiry date is unaffected (both start at conclusion), but the citation in the clause must be right.
3. **Article 6(1) paragraph letters** — confirm that withdrawal information is point **(h)**, cost-of-return is **(f)**, service-cost liability is **(j)** and no-right/loss-of-right is **(k)**.
4. **Article 8(4)** — confirm the model-instruction facility and the exact list of Article 6(1) points it covers.
5. **Article 14(4)(a)** and **Article 16(a)/(m)** — confirm paragraph letters and the precise wording of the consent/acknowledgement conditions, since these are the clauses the trader will have to prove.
6. **Article 11(2)** — confirm the paragraph number for the "sent before expiry" rule.
7. **Language and national law** — take the text from the language version required by the Member State of sale, and check the national transposition for (i) the counting rule (whether the trigger day is excluded and whether expiry is at midnight), (ii) any language requirements, and (iii) any mandatory pre-contractual form. Article 4 (level of harmonisation) means a Member State may not maintain or introduce provisions diverging from the directive, including more or less stringent ones, so the 14-day period and the Article 10 extension should be uniform — but the counting mechanics and the delivery of the information are transposed nationally and must be checked per market.

## 8. Limits of this answer

- **Directive-only.** It states the EU default for distance and off-premises contracts. It does not state any national transposition, and it is not an opinion on the law of any specific Member State.
- **Default periods plus the Article 10 extension and the Article 16 loss/exclusion rules only.** It is not a survey of every sectoral exception (timeshare, package travel, financial services, consumer credit and similar sit under separate instruments).
- **Mixed contracts.** A contract having as its object both goods and services is a "sales contract" under Art. 2(5), so the goods trigger in Art. 9(2)(a) applies. Where the goods are merely ancillary to a service (materials consumed in a repair), the contract is a service contract and the conclusion trigger applies. The trader must classify each product line and pick the matching clause; a single blended clause for a mixed catalogue will be wrong for part of it.
- **Not covered:** whether a specific online checkout meets the Art. 8(1) plain-and-intelligible-language standard, or the Art. 8(2) reduced-information regime for limited-space/limited-time distance communication (SMS, short-form app checkout), which needs separate drafting.

## 9. Compliance checklist for the drafting owner

- [ ] Clause states **14 days** for each contract type, with the correct trigger (possession vs. conclusion).
- [ ] Sub-rules for separate deliveries / multiple lots / regular deliveries added where the catalogue requires them.
- [ ] "Sending before expiry is sufficient" sentence present.
- [ ] Annex I(B) model form attached and the trader's contact details filled in.
- [ ] Art. 16 exclusions and loss-of-right statements present where applicable, with the consent/acknowledgement mechanics built into the checkout for services and digital content.
- [ ] Art. 10 exposure checked: is the withdrawal information inside the pre-contractual pack, in every channel?
- [ ] 14-day reimbursement promise stated consistently with Art. 13(1) and the Art. 13(3) withholding right.
- [ ] Text verified against the official Annex I(A)/I(B) and the correct language version for each market.

question: Y131
answer:
FAIR-TRIAL TRAINING MODULE — ARTICLE 6 § 2, ECHR, TEXT AS AMENDED THROUGH PROTOCOL No. 15

=== 1. THE QUOTATION TO BE USED IN THE MODULE (verbatim) ===

Reproduce exactly as follows, retaining the paragraph number and the Article heading:

    ARTICLE 6
    Right to a fair trial

    2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed
    innocent until proved guilty according to law.

Run as a single line in the module (line break above merely mirrors the printed page):

    "2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

If the paragraph number is carried by the module's own layout (e.g. a numbered list or a marginal reference), the quotable sentence alone is:

    "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

Both forms are used below; they are the same text and must not be reworded.

=== 2. PROVENANCE — WHAT "AS AMENDED THROUGH PROTOCOL No. 15" MEANS HERE ===

The source is the European Court of Human Rights' own consolidated English text of the Convention, whose front matter reads (verbatim from the fetched document):

    "European Convention on Human Rights
     as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15
     supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16"

    "The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010."

Source document: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (fetched 2026-11-23; sha256 f4608f7ed2d5). Article 6 appears at the pages carrying the running numbers 10–11 of that PDF.

Protocol No. 15 identity, from the fetched treaty text: "Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (CETS No. 213)", Strasbourg, 24.VI.2013 (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG; sha256 57f7f5bb1c0e). Its Article 7 provides for entry into force on the first day of the month following the expiry of three months after all High Contracting Parties expressed consent to be bound; the ECHR consolidated text records the resulting date as 1 August 2021.

=== 3. WHY THE PROTOCOL No. 15 FRAMING DOES NOT ALTER THIS CLAUSE ===

From the fetched Protocol No. 15 text, the operative amendments are confined to:
- Article 1 — insertion of a new recital at the end of the Preamble (subsidiarity / margin of appreciation);
- Article 2 — insertion of a new Article 21 § 2 (candidates under 65), renumbering of Article 21 §§ 2–3 to §§ 3–4, deletion of Article 23 § 2 and renumbering of Article 23 §§ 3–4 to §§ 2–3;
- Article 3 — deletion from Article 30 of the words "unless one of the parties to the case objects";
- Article 4 — amendment of the admissibility time-limit (six months to four months), with a six-month transitional provision in Article 8 § 3;
- Article 5 — amendment of Article 35 § 3 (b) ("significant disadvantage" criterion);
- Articles 6–9 — final clauses.

No article of Protocol No. 15 amends Article 6. The presumption of innocence clause is therefore textually identical in the pre- and post-Protocol No. 15 consolidated versions. The module should say so expressly, so that a trainee is not left with the impression that the presumption was recently reworded. Suggested module sentence: "Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), in force since 1 August 2021, amended the Preamble, Articles 21, 23, 30 and 35 of the Convention; it did not amend Article 6. The text of Article 6 § 2 quoted here is identical before and after that Protocol."

=== 4. WHAT THE PRESUMPTION IS (answer to the third ask) ===

The presumption that applies to everyone charged with a criminal offence is the presumption of innocence, guaranteed by Article 6 § 2 ECHR. The Convention's own words are those in section 1. The ECHR's Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb) states: "Paragraph 2 of Article 6 embodies the principle of the presumption of innocence." For the training module's explanatory (non-quoted) layer, the same Guide, citing Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain (1988, § 77), identifies three requirements: (1) members of the court must not start with the preconceived idea that the accused has committed the offence charged; (2) the burden of proof is on the prosecution; (3) any doubt should benefit the accused. Mark this clearly as explanatory case-law content, visually separated from the verbatim Convention quotation.

=== 5. CITATION STRINGS (pick per the module's house style) ===

- Full: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 6 § 2, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 (Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021), Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights consolidated text.
- Short: ECHR, Article 6 § 2.
- With URL and date: ECHR, Article 6 § 2, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (consolidated text as amended through Protocol No. 15, in force 1 August 2021; accessed [insert date]).
- Note on numbering: the Convention's own text prints "2."; ECHR usage cites "Article 6 § 2". "Article 6(2)" is a domestic-style rendering and is acceptable in national training material, but the module should standardise on one form — recommended: Article 6 § 2 in the running text, with "Article 6(2)" given once in parentheses on first use if the audience expects it.

=== 6. QUOTATION-INTEGRITY CHECKLIST (apply before publication) ===

1. "proved", not "proven".
2. No comma before "until"; no comma after "offence".
3. "offence" (British spelling), not "offense".
4. "shall be presumed innocent" — not "is presumed innocent", not "must be presumed".
5. "according to law" — not "in accordance with law", not "according to the law".
6. Terminal full stop included when the sentence is quoted as a sentence.
7. "Everyone charged with a criminal offence" — no "person", no "accused person" substitution.
8. Do not add quotation marks inside the quotation; do not italicise words within it.
9. If the module abbreviates, use an ellipsis only outside the sentence; this sentence must never be truncated — truncating it at "presumed innocent" would delete the "until proved guilty according to law" qualifier, which is part of the guarantee.
10. Where the module uses the ECHR's PDF pagination, note that the printed page break falls between "presumed" and "innocent"; this is a typesetting artefact and must not be reproduced as a hyphen or a break inside the quote in web output.

=== 7. SCOPE — WHAT THIS CLAUSE IS NOT ===

Article 6 § 2 consists of that one sentence and nothing more; there is no second sentence of paragraph 2 to quote. Do not attribute to the text of Article 6 § 2 the burden-of-proof rule, the benefit-of-the-doubt rule, or rules on legal presumptions and reverse burdens: those are requirements derived by the Court from the clause (see section 4), not words of the Convention. Article 6 § 1 (fair and public hearing) and Article 6 § 3 (minimum rights of everyone charged with a criminal offence) are separate paragraphs and must be quoted separately if the module needs them; both are available verbatim in the same fetched consolidated text.

=== 8. OPEN ITEMS FOR THE MODULE OWNER (flagged, not resolved by this deliverable) ===

(a) Language version: the quotation above is the English text. No French consolidated text was retrieved for this task, so no French version is reproduced here; if the module is bilingual, the French authentic text must be taken from the ECHR's French consolidated version (Convention_FRA) and verified character-by-character before publication — do not back-translate.
(b) The module owner should confirm the required citation style from section 5 and the required date-of-access stamp.
(c) Confirm whether the module needs Article 6 § 1 and § 3 for context; if so, quote them separately from the same consolidated source.
(d) No jurisdiction-specific reservations or declarations affecting Article 6 § 2 are recorded in the fetched sources; if the module is delivered in a State Party with a relevant declaration, check the Council of Europe Treaty Office chart of signatures and ratifications for that State before publication.

question: Y132
answer:
Governing rule text (16 CFR Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21; 2026 CFR edition):

- 16 CFR § 3.12(a): 'A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint.'
- 16 CFR § 3.21(b): 'Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference.'

Assumptions required by the question:

1. Single-respondent adjudication. The sole respondent is therefore the 'last answering respondent' for purposes of § 3.21(b). There is no other respondent whose answer could start the 10-day period later.
2. The respondent uses the entire answer period. The answer is filed on the last permissible day: day 14 after service of the complaint.
3. The ALJ uses the entire period allowed after that answer. The scheduling conference is held on the last permissible day: day 10 after the answer is filed.
4. Only these two stated periods are counted. The separate 2-day deadline after the conference for the prehearing scheduling order under § 3.21(c)(1), the final prehearing conference under § 3.21(e), and the 5-month or 8-month evidentiary-hearing dates under § 3.11(a)(4) are not included.

Calculation:

- Service of complaint to answer: 14 days.
- Answer to scheduling conference: 10 days.
- Combined interval: 14 + 10 = 24 days.

Result: the combined interval from service of the complaint to the scheduling conference is 24 calendar days. Equivalently, the conference must be held no later than 24 days after service if the respondent answers on the final permissible day and the ALJ schedules the conference on the final permissible day.

Counting convention: the rule states the periods in 'days' and does not specify business days, so the periods are treated as calendar days for this computation. The rule's general time-computation convention excludes the triggering event day and includes the last day, subject to weekend/holiday extension rules; because no actual service date is supplied, the answer is the maximum nominal interval measured from service, not a specific calendar date. If the 24th day fell on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, the actual last day could roll to the next business day under the applicable computation rule, but that would be an application of a separate time-computation rule, not an addition to either of the two stated periods, and the question directs use of only those two periods.
